spellbook_fire_spark.name: Spellbook of Fire Spark
spellbook_fire_spark.lore: When Zeus had hidden fire from mankind, Prometheus stole it back from Olympus in the pithy stalk of a giant fennel, where an ember may smoulder for hours and never burn through. Every student of fire begins with a small copy of that theft, and in these first pages he learns to throw a single dart of flame, hot as a candle and about as large.

spellbook_fire_bolt.name: Spellbook of Fire Bolt
spellbook_fire_bolt.lore: The Chimera, which had a lion's head, a goat's body and a serpent's tail, breathed fire over all Lycia until Bellerophon flew above it on Pegasus and thrust lead into its throat upon the point of his lance, and the creature's own breath melted the metal and choked it. That breath is taught again in this primer, as one hard bolt of flame.

spellbook_fireball.name: Spellbook of Fireball
spellbook_fireball.lore: Archimedes, when the fleet of Rome closed upon Syracuse in 212 before Christ, is said by later writers to have lined the walls with shields of polished bronze and turned the noon sun upon the ships until their timbers took fire. Engineers dispute even now whether such a thing could be done, but the battle-mages who wrote this book found a way of their own, by which every enemy in sight burns at once.

spellbook_meteor.name: Spellbook of Meteor
spellbook_meteor.lore: On 7 November 1492 a stone weighing more than a hundred kilograms fell with a clap of thunder into the wheat of Ensisheim in Alsace, and so great was the fear of the townsfolk that they chained it within the church, lest it depart as it had come. By the words of this tome another such stone is called out of heaven, and it falls upon all that stand in sight of the caster.

spellbook_cataclysm.name: Spellbook of Cataclysm
spellbook_cataclysm.lore: Five cities stood upon the plain of the Jordan, and Abraham pleaded for them until the Lord would spare them for the sake of ten righteous men, but ten could not be found. Brimstone and fire rained out of heaven, and in the morning he saw the smoke go up as from a furnace. In memory of that rain the last and greatest spell of fire brings down five burning stones, one after another.

spellbook_frost_touch.name: Spellbook of Frost Touch
spellbook_frost_touch.lore: Hans Christian Andersen told in 1844 of a boy into whose heart went a splinter of a goblin's mirror, so that it became a lump of ice, and how the Snow Queen kissed him twice and he felt the cold no more. A touch like hers is the first lesson in frost, and it bites sorely and will sometimes slow the one who feels it.

spellbook_cold_bolt.name: Spellbook of Cold Bolt
spellbook_cold_bolt.lore: Skadi the giantess came down in full armour to avenge her father, and the gods made peace by granting her a husband, whom she must choose by his feet alone. She chose the wrong god, and in the end went home to hunt on skis among her mountains. From her this tome takes its manner of shooting, with a shard of ice that leaves its quarry slow.

spellbook_ice_storm.name: Spellbook of Ice Storm
spellbook_ice_storm.lore: Hail was the seventh plague of Egypt, the worst since that land became a nation, and fire ran along the ground in the midst of it. It broke every tree and beat down the flax and the barley in all the fields save those of Goshen. He who reads this spell aright brings that sky within a single room, and every enemy he can see must stand beneath its stones.

spellbook_cone_of_cold.name: Spellbook of Cone of Cold
spellbook_cone_of_cold.lore: Dante went down to the bottom of Hell looking for fire and found ice, for there the traitors lie frozen to their necks in the lake Cocytus, and Satan stands locked to the chest in the midst, beating six wings whose wind keeps all the lake hard. One beat of those wings is the last secret of frost, and whatever stands close before the caster is frozen through.

spellbook_spark.name: Spellbook of Spark
spellbook_spark.lore: Mariners in the storm would sometimes see blue fire hissing on the mastheads, and they blessed it as the sign of Saint Erasmus their patron, whom they called Elmo, for it meant that the worst was past. The apprentice of lightning first learns to draw down that same fire to the ends of his fingers and to let it leap.

spellbook_lightning_bolt.name: Spellbook of Lightning Bolt
spellbook_lightning_bolt.lore: Salmoneus, king of Elis, desired to be worshipped as Zeus, and he drove through his city trailing kettles of bronze for thunder and flinging torches for lightning, until the god answered him with the true bolt and destroyed him. It is the true bolt that this tome teaches, a white line passing through everything that stands in its path.

spellbook_chain_lightning.name: Spellbook of Chain Lightning
spellbook_chain_lightning.lore: The Abbe Nollet in 1746 joined some two hundred Carthusian monks in one great ring with lengths of iron wire and closed it upon a charged Leyden jar, and all the monks leapt in the same instant. His art is bettered in these pages, for here the bolt needs no wire and springs from one enemy to the next, a little weaker at each leap.

spellbook_storm_of_vengeance.name: Spellbook of Storm of Vengeance
spellbook_storm_of_vengeance.lore: While Samuel was yet offering the lamb at Mizpah the Philistines drew near to make war upon Israel, but that day the Lord thundered against them with a mighty sound, and they were confounded and put to rout before a blow was struck. With such a voice the last spell of storm breaks overhead, so that all in sight are smitten and many of them are left stunned.

spellbook_magic_dart.name: Spellbook of Magic Dart
spellbook_magic_dart.lore: In the year 1307, as the tale has it, an Austrian bailiff commanded William Tell to shoot an apple from his own son's head, and he split it with his crossbow, having a second bolt ready for the bailiff. That first bolt is the first spell of every apprentice, a single dart of force that flies and does not miss.

spellbook_magic_missile.name: Spellbook of Magic Missile
spellbook_magic_missile.lore: Three arrows were the sign agreed between Jonathan and his friend David, who lay hidden in a field from King Saul: they would fall beside a certain stone, and by what Jonathan called to the lad who fetched them David should know whether to stay or flee. After that pattern this book looses three darts of force together, and no lad need gather them.

spellbook_force_barrage.name: Spellbook of Force Barrage
spellbook_force_barrage.lore: David put off the king's armour and went down to the brook, where he chose five smooth stones for his shepherd's bag, though in the end he had need of one only. The other four live on in this tome, which teaches how five darts of force may be thrown in a breath, and no helm of bronze has been found that will turn them.

spellbook_force_storm.name: Spellbook of Force Storm
spellbook_force_storm.lore: For seven days seven priests bore seven horns of rams about Jericho, and on the seventh day they went round it seven times, and when the people shouted the wall fell down flat, though no hand had touched it. In remembrance of them this spell throws seven darts of pure force, and no wall, shield or ward has yet turned one aside.

spellbook_annihilation.name: Spellbook of Annihilation
spellbook_annihilation.lore: After the Black Death the painters gave Death a scythe and showed him mowing pope, king and ploughman in one swath. A reaper takes the ripe ears and bruises those that are green, and the stroke taught in this tome falls in like manner, for creatures already failing are gone altogether and those still strong are each cut nearly in half.

spellbook_acid_dart.name: Spellbook of Acid Dart
spellbook_acid_dart.lore: The alchemists made aqua fortis, which is strong water, by heating saltpetre with vitriol and gathering the red fumes, and since it eats silver and leaves gold it was loved by every assayer and dreaded by every forger. A splash of it is the dart that they taught to their apprentices, and it continues to burn long after it has landed.

spellbook_acid_arrow.name: Spellbook of Acid Arrow
spellbook_acid_arrow.lore: Out of green vitriol, roasted in a sealed retort, the alchemists of old distilled a heavy liquor which they named oil of vitriol and ranked first among acids, for it chars cloth and does worse to flesh. The maker of this tome shaped that oil into an arrow, and a wound that is given by it goes on eating for a long while afterward.

spellbook_dissolution.name: Spellbook of Dissolution
spellbook_dissolution.lore: Royal water, which is aqua regia, is the only acid that will dissolve gold. When German soldiers entered Copenhagen in 1940, the chemist George de Hevesy melted away two Nobel medals in a jar of it and left the jar upon a shelf, where they passed it by, and after the war the gold was recovered and cast anew. If even gold must yield to such water, it is small wonder that the last spell of acid spares nothing.

spellbook_cure_light.name: Spellbook of Cure Light Wounds
spellbook_cure_light.lore: When Menelaus took an arrow through the belt, as the Iliad tells, the Greeks sent for Machaon the son of Asclepius, who drew the shaft, sucked the hurt clean and spread upon it the soothing herbs that Chiron the centaur gave his father long before. So much, and no more, is taught to the healer upon the battlefield, to cleanse and close a small wound.

spellbook_cure_wounds.name: Spellbook of Cure Wounds
spellbook_cure_wounds.lore: Ibn Sina the Persian, whom Europe called Avicenna, completed his Canon of Medicine in 1025 in five books, and six hundred years afterward the masters of Montpellier and Padua were teaching from it still. Out of its pages is drawn the reader given to temple physicians in their second year, and by this they learn the working cure for an ordinary wound.

spellbook_heal.name: Spellbook of Heal
spellbook_heal.lore: King Telephus bore in his thigh a wound from Achilles that would not close, and an oracle declared that he who wounded should heal. Achilles protested that he was no physician, but Odysseus saw that the spear itself was meant, and rust scraped from it into the wound made the king whole. Of such power is the major healing word in this tome.

spellbook_greater_heal.name: Spellbook of Greater Heal
spellbook_greater_heal.lore: In the hall of Asclepius at Epidaurus the sick would lie down at evening to await the god in their dreams, while his sacred serpents and dogs moved among them licking their wounds, and the cures were graven upon stone, where some may still be read. All the healing of such a night is gathered here into a single moment.

spellbook_resurrection.name: Spellbook of Resurrection
spellbook_resurrection.lore: Lazarus of Bethany had lain four days in the tomb, and his sister warned of the smell when Jesus came to it. But Jesus, who had wept for him, called him by name in a loud voice, and the dead man came forth bound still in his grave cloths. This liturgy makes that prayer beforehand, so that the next death that comes for its caster is refused.

spellbook_sleep.name: Spellbook of Sleep
spellbook_sleep.lore: So fair was Endymion the shepherd that the Moon entreated Zeus to keep him as he was, and he was given sleep without age or ending in a cave upon Mount Latmus, where she visits him nightly. By the gentlest of all enchantments the student learns to send one creature after him into slumber, though for a far shorter space.

spellbook_mass_sleep.name: Spellbook of Mass Sleep
spellbook_mass_sleep.lore: Saul hunted David with three thousand men and made his camp upon the hill of Hachilah, and there a deep sleep from the Lord fell upon them all. David came among them in the night, took the spear and the jar of water from beside the king's head, and departed unhindered. When these words are spoken the same sleep descends on every enemy in sight.

spellbook_deep_slumber.name: Spellbook of Deep Slumber
spellbook_deep_slumber.lore: A princess pricked her finger, in the tale that Charles Perrault printed in 1697, and the good fairy went through the castle touching with her wand guards, cooks and horses, and the very spits on the fire with their partridges, until all were still for a hundred years. With a sleep as deep the last spell of slumber holds a whole room fast.

spellbook_slow.name: Spellbook of Slow
spellbook_slow.lore: The hare in Aesop's fable was so certain of the race that he lay down by the road to sleep, while the tortoise walked on and never stopped. By this primer a traveller may change places with a swifter foe, for his enemy must go for a good while at the tortoise's pace and he himself may be the hare.

spellbook_mass_slow.name: Spellbook of Mass Slow
spellbook_mass_slow.lore: The chariots of Pharaoh followed Israel over the dry bed of the sea, and in the morning watch the Lord looked forth from the pillar of fire and cloud and clogged their wheels, so that they drove heavily and the charioteers cried to one another to flee. When these words are read every enemy in sight is bogged down with the like weight.

spellbook_time_freeze.name: Spellbook of Time Freeze
spellbook_time_freeze.lore: Pompeii was buried by Vesuvius in a day and a night of the year 79, and when Giuseppe Fiorelli, from 1863 onward, poured plaster into the hollows of the ash he found its people as death had left them, a man shielding his face and a dog straining at its chain. Even so, for a few heartbeats, this spell arrests every creature upon the floor.

spellbook_hold_monster.name: Spellbook of Hold Monster
spellbook_hold_monster.lore: Gleipnir, the ribbon that bound Fenrir, was made from the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish and the spittle of a bird, and for that reason none of those six is found in the world any longer. He who studies here may pay out a length of the ribbon to bind one creature.

spellbook_paralyze.name: Spellbook of Paralyze
spellbook_paralyze.lore: For the death of Baldr the gods bound Loki in a cave across three sharp stones, beneath a serpent that drips venom upon his face. His wife Sigyn catches it in a bowl, but when she turns to empty the bowl he writhes until the earth quakes, and yet he cannot rise. The stronger binding will hold one enemy as fast as Loki is held.

spellbook_mass_paralyze.name: Spellbook of Mass Paralyze
spellbook_mass_paralyze.lore: Perseus came home bearing the Gorgon's head in a bag and found King Polydectes at table with his court, pressing still for the hand of the hero's mother. He bade his friends cover their eyes and held up the head, and the king and all his guests sit there in stone to this hour. With this tome one may learn to hold a whole room as still.

spellbook_fear.name: Spellbook of Fear
spellbook_fear.lore: The shield that Agamemnon bore to war had ten rings of bronze, and the Gorgon glared from the midst with Fear and Rout on either hand, and for centuries afterward the soldiers of Greece painted that face upon their own. This spell sets it before one enemy, who forgets the battle and runs away.

spellbook_terror.name: Spellbook of Terror
spellbook_terror.lore: With three hundred men Gideon went out against the host of Midian, and to each he gave a trumpet and a torch hidden in a jar of clay. At midnight they broke the jars and blew and shouted, and all the camp awoke crying and fled. The Word of Terror holds that midnight in it, and every enemy in sight of the speaker runs.

spellbook_confusion.name: Spellbook of Confusion
spellbook_confusion.lore: Ate, the spirit of folly, beguiled Zeus himself into a rash oath, and he took her by the hair and flung her out of Olympus for ever. Since then she has dwelt with mortals, walking on their heads with feet so soft that they do not feel her, and by this spell she is set upon the shoulders of one enemy.

spellbook_madness.name: Spellbook of Madness
spellbook_madness.lore: Nebuchadnezzar walked upon the roof of his palace glorying in the Babylon he had built, and in that hour his reason departed from him. He was driven from among men and ate grass as oxen do, and his hair grew like eagles' feathers until seven times had passed over him. The Word of Madness breaks in that manner every mind in sight.

spellbook_mage_armor.name: Spellbook of Mage Armor
spellbook_mage_armor.lore: While he lay in prison under a Roman guard, the apostle Paul wrote to the Ephesians of the arms he saw before him, belt and breastplate, boots, shield, helmet and sword, and by them he signified truth, righteousness, peace, faith, salvation and the word. A wizard's first defence is an armour as unseen as these, and blows land more softly through it.

spellbook_magic_shield.name: Spellbook of Magic Shield
spellbook_magic_shield.lore: In five layers Hephaestus forged the shield of Achilles, two of bronze, two of tin and one of gold, and the spear of Aeneas broke through two and was stayed in the gold. Those who study this tome learn to raise a shield of that fashion out of the empty air, and it turns hard blows for a good while.

spellbook_stoneskin.name: Spellbook of Stoneskin
spellbook_stoneskin.lore: Siegfried bathed in the blood of the dragon he had slain, and his skin grew hard as horn against every blade, save where a linden leaf had clung between his shoulders, and Hagen learned of the place and slew him. This spell leaves no leaf, but hardens the whole body and outlasts every other guard.

spellbook_haste.name: Spellbook of Haste
spellbook_haste.lore: Hermes was born at dawn, by noon had fashioned the lyre, and by evening had stolen the cattle of his brother Apollo, and the golden winged sandals called talaria bore him over land and sea as swiftly as the wind. This spell laces them upon its caster's feet, so that for a short while he acts twice to his enemy's once.

spellbook_greater_haste.name: Spellbook of Greater Haste
spellbook_greater_haste.lore: Thialfi, the servant of Thor, was the swiftest runner among men, yet in the hall of Utgard-Loki he raced a boy named Hugi three times, and each time the boy had turned at the post before Thialfi could reach it, for Hugi was the thought of the giant king himself. The speed taught in this tome comes nearer to Hugi's, and it lasts long.

spellbook_invisibility.name: Spellbook of Invisibility
spellbook_invisibility.lore: A shepherd named Gyges, of whom Plato tells, found a ring of gold upon a corpse within a horse of bronze in a cleft of the earth, and when he turned it inward it hid him from all eyes, so that he slew the king of Lydia and took the throne. The spell hides its caster likewise, until he strikes the first blow.

spellbook_greater_invisibility.name: Spellbook of Greater Invisibility
spellbook_greater_invisibility.lore: From Alberich the dwarf Siegfried won the cloak of hiding called Tarnkappe, and when King Gunther must win Queen Brunhild at spear, stone and leaping, Siegfried stood beside him unseen and did every deed while Gunther made the show of it. This greater spell has the virtue of that cloak, and it holds through all the fight.

spellbook_displacement.name: Spellbook of Displacement
spellbook_displacement.lore: Helen never came to Troy at all, if the poet Stesichorus sang truly, for the gods sent a phantom with Paris while she waited out the war in Egypt, and two hosts fought ten years for a shape of cloud. Such a shape may be raised from these pages to stand at the caster's side, and the blows meant for him go wide.

spellbook_reflect.name: Spellbook of Spell Reflect
spellbook_reflect.lore: Athena lent Perseus a shield of polished bronze, since the gaze of Medusa turned men to stone, and he walked backward to the sleeping Gorgon and struck by her image there, never looking upon her. In this tome one may learn the bearing of that shield, by which curses and hostile enchantments are often turned back upon their senders.

spellbook_detect_magic.name: Spellbook of Detect Magic
spellbook_detect_magic.lore: In the breastpiece of the high priest of Israel lay the Urim and the Thummim, by which he put questions to God and was answered, as it seems, with yes or no. Their very shape is now forgotten, but this tract has kept their manner of asking, and of each enchanted thing that lies in sight it inquires whether it be blessed or cursed.

spellbook_identify.name: Spellbook of Identify
spellbook_identify.lore: Archimedes was bidden by King Hiero to learn, without melting a certain crown, whether the goldsmith had mixed silver into it, and as his bath overflowed he saw the way and ran home crying that he had found it. By a like discernment this book will tell, of all that lies in view or rides in the pack, what is blessed and what is cursed.

spellbook_omnisight.name: Spellbook of Omnisight
spellbook_omnisight.lore: From the high seat Hlidskjalf Odin looks out over all the worlds and understands whatever he sees, and each dawn he sends forth two ravens, Thought and Memory, who bring him tidings by breakfast. The sight of an archmage is made after his, and before it all things on the floor, in the pack and on the body declare their blessing or their curse.

spellbook_detect_monsters.name: Spellbook of Detect Monsters
spellbook_detect_monsters.lore: The king of Aram compassed Dothan by night to take the prophet Elisha, and at waking the prophet's servant despaired, until Elisha prayed that the young man's eyes be opened and he saw the hills filled with horses and chariots of fire. These words open the eyes in the same fashion, and every living thing upon the floor is shown for a while.

spellbook_foresight.name: Spellbook of Foresight
spellbook_foresight.lore: Cassandra of Troy had the gift of prophecy from Apollo, and when she refused him he laid this curse upon it, that she should see truly and never be believed, so that men laughed when she warned them of the wooden horse. The reader of this book receives her sight without her curse, and every creature on the floor is known for a long while.

spellbook_mapping.name: Spellbook of Mapping
spellbook_mapping.lore: Claudius Ptolemy of Alexandria, about the year 150, set down some eight thousand places by latitude and longitude and showed how the round world might be drawn upon a flat sheet. His Geography was lost to the West for a thousand years and remade every chart on its return, and by his art this spell draws a whole floor at once.

spellbook_greater_mapping.name: Spellbook of Greater Mapping
spellbook_greater_mapping.lore: At the Norman court of Palermo al-Idrisi laboured fifteen years, questioning every traveller who came ashore, and in 1154 he gave King Roger the world engraved on a disc of silver, with a book that told of every region. A master of mapping is as thorough as he, and by this spell walls, creatures and treasure are all laid open.

spellbook_blink.name: Spellbook of Blink
spellbook_blink.lore: Philip baptised a courtier of Ethiopia in a pool beside the desert road to Gaza, and as they came up out of the water the Spirit caught him away, so that he found himself at Azotus, twenty miles off. The first spell of journeying carries the caster as suddenly, and like Philip he has no choosing of the place to which he goes.

spellbook_phase_door.name: Spellbook of Phase Door
spellbook_phase_door.lore: King Sveigdir of Sweden was going home drunken at sunset, as the saga relates, when a dwarf beneath a boulder great as a house called him in to meet Odin. He ran into the stone and it closed upon him, and he was never seen again. Here one may learn to walk into stone as he did, and afterward to come out again.

spellbook_gate.name: Spellbook of Gate
spellbook_gate.lore: Jacob laid his head upon a stone and dreamed of a ladder set between earth and heaven with angels going up and down upon it, and he woke in dread and named that place the gate of heaven, as Babylon is named the gate of God. The word that is written here opens a door of that kind, and out of it steps a mighty ally.

spellbook_turn_undead.name: Spellbook of Turn Undead
spellbook_turn_undead.lore: Before they sleep the monks sing Compline, and since the seventh century at the least its hymn has besought the Creator to drive far away the dreams and phantoms of the night. This compendium restores the full weight of those words, so that when they are spoken the dead in sight are burned with light and flee from the speaker.

spellbook_sunburst.name: Spellbook of Sunburst
spellbook_sunburst.lore: Peter, James and John were led by Jesus up a high mountain, which tradition names Tabor, and there his face shone as the sun and his raiment grew white as light, and the three fell upon their faces. The greatest of the holy spells borrows one moment of that brightness, and all the dead within sight of it are seared and scattered.

spellbook_polymorph.name: Spellbook of Polymorph
spellbook_polymorph.lore: Lycaon, king of Arcadia, would prove whether the traveller at his table were truly Zeus, and set human flesh before him. The god brought down the roof, and as the king fled over the fields his robes became fur and his arms legs, and his cry was a howl. So does this spell remake one creature, and often into some lesser thing.

spellbook_mass_polymorph.name: Spellbook of Mass Polymorph
spellbook_mass_polymorph.lore: Leto came with her newborn twins to a pond of Lycia and would have drunk, but the peasants who cut reeds there forbade her and trod the water to mud for spite. She prayed that they might dwell in that pond for ever, and frogs they became. Whoever learns her prayer from this tome may turn a roomful of enemies small and feeble.

spellbook_drain_life.name: Spellbook of Drain Life
spellbook_drain_life.lore: The physician and the worm had but one name in Old English, which was leech. Doctors of the Middle Ages would set the creature on the sick to draw away bad blood, and France alone brought in forty million a year in the 1830s. The art written here turns their trade about, and draws the life out of an enemy and into the caster.

spellbook_soul_drain.name: Spellbook of Soul Drain
spellbook_soul_drain.lore: Antaeus the giant wrestled every traveller through Libya and roofed a temple with the skulls of the vanquished, for the Earth was his mother and he rose the stronger each time he was thrown upon her, until Heracles held him aloft and his strength ebbed. By this dark art an enemy is made to serve the caster as the Earth served Antaeus.

spellbook_light.name: Spellbook of Light
spellbook_light.lore: The first words that God speaks in Scripture are a command, which Jerome rendered in two words of Latin, fiat lux, and there was light before ever sun or moon was made, or anything to see by it. The simplest spell in the library says those words again, and the dark draws back from you on every side and stays back a good while.

spellbook_knock.name: Spellbook of Knock
spellbook_knock.lore: Ali Baba was cutting wood when he heard the captain of forty thieves speak two words before a rock, and saw it open. His brother went in by the same craft and then forgot the words, and called in vain on every other grain he knew. The right grain is named in this book, and at its name a locked chest near at hand springs open.

spellbook_cleanse.name: Spellbook of Cleanse
spellbook_cleanse.lore: Naaman, who commanded the armies of Aram, was a leper, and it angered him that Elisha sent word from within doors to wash seven times in Jordan, when Damascus had fairer rivers. But his servants persuaded him, and his flesh came again as clean as a child's. A single reading of these words will likewise lift a single affliction.

spellbook_empower.name: Spellbook of Empower
spellbook_empower.lore: Roland, as he lay dying at Roncevaux, smote Durendal upon a rock lest an enemy should bear it, but the sword would not break. The folk of the Pyrenees still show a gap forty metres wide in the mountain wall and say that this was the rock, and here the caster learns to store one such stroke in the next blow that he deals.

spellbook_levitate.name: Spellbook of Levitate
spellbook_levitate.lore: Joseph of Cupertino, a Franciscan friar who died in 1663, was so slow at his books that he was made a priest only because he was asked the one question he knew, and for this he is the patron of all who are examined. Yet at prayer he rose into the air seventy times before witnesses, and as he rose the caster shall rise, clear of pits and snares.

spellbook_teleport_away.name: Spellbook of Teleport Away
spellbook_teleport_away.lore: The men of Athens might vote once a year to be rid of a citizen, each scratching a name upon a potsherd called an ostrakon, and he who had most must depart within ten days for ten years. This spell gives that sentence against the nearest enemy, who is at once elsewhere, but where no enemy is near it is the caster who goes.

spellbook_smite.name: Spellbook of Smite
spellbook_smite.lore: In Silene of Libya, says the Golden Legend, there was a dragon that poisoned all the land and was fed first on sheep and afterward on children chosen by lot. When the lot fell upon the king's daughter, George came riding, crossed himself and ran the beast through. His lance is this spell, and no hide or ward can lessen it.

spellbook_dispel_magic.name: Spellbook of Dispel Magic
spellbook_dispel_magic.lore: In Rome, so an old legend says, Simon the Magician boasted before the emperor that he would fly, and when he leapt from a tower of wood the spirits bore him over the Forum, but the apostle Peter knelt and prayed, and they let him fall. What that prayer wrought is taught here, and at its word every enchantment upon one enemy drops away.

spellbook_counterspell.name: Spellbook of Counterspell
spellbook_counterspell.lore: Odysseus knew that the Sirens sang from a meadow heaped with the bones of sailors who had listened, and he stopped the ears of his crew with beeswax and was himself lashed to the mast, so that he alone heard them and lived. This spell is both wax and cord, and charms, terrors and confusions slide for a time from him who casts it.

spellbook_summon_guardian.name: Spellbook of Summon Guardian
spellbook_summon_guardian.lore: A lion came limping into the monastery of Jerome at Bethlehem, and while the other monks fled he drew a thorn from its paw and bound the hurt, and it remained all its days to guard the monastery's donkey. A beast of like faithfulness will answer the caster's call, though it will not always be a lion.

spellbook_disintegrate.name: Spellbook of Disintegrate
spellbook_disintegrate.lore: Nebuchadnezzar saw in dream an image with head of gold, breast of silver, thighs of bronze and feet of iron mixed with clay, until a stone cut by no human hand smote the feet, and all became chaff upon the wind. That stone is cast by this spell, and one time in two it leaves nothing at all of the one it strikes.

spellbook_power_word_kill.name: Spellbook of Power Word Kill
spellbook_power_word_kill.lore: The maker of the golem, so the legends say, wrote upon its brow the Hebrew word emet, which is truth, and the clay stood up, and to end its life he rubbed away one letter, leaving met, which is dead. The shorter word is kept in this tome, and to a creature weakened enough it is the last word that is ever heard.

spellbook_wish.name: Spellbook of Wish
spellbook_wish.lore: Midas asked that his touch turn all to gold, and nearly starved. The Sibyl of Cumae asked as many years as she held grains of sand but forgot to ask for youth, and withered until she hung in a jar longing to die. This tome has therefore one blank page, and the world itself chooses the boon, which is safer for the one who wishes.

spellbook_imprisonment.name: Spellbook of Imprisonment
spellbook_imprisonment.lore: A fisherman in the Arabian Nights drew up a jar of copper, stopped with lead beneath the seal of Solomon, and when he had prised it open there rose from it in smoke a jinni who had lain eighteen hundred years within. This spell is the stopper of that jar, and by it one enemy is shut in stone for a very long time.

spellbook_banishment.name: Spellbook of Banishment
spellbook_banishment.lore: When war arose in heaven Michael and his angels strove with the dragon, and the dragon and his angels did not prevail, and no place was found any longer for them there. A lesser sentence of that kind is written here, and by it a demon, fey or spirit must return to the country whence it came.

spellbook_army_of_darkness.name: Spellbook of Army of Darkness
spellbook_army_of_darkness.lore: The Einherjar are those fallen warriors whom Odin gathers into Valhalla, where each morning they arm and hew one another down, and each evening rise up whole and go in to supper. The maker of this tome took their rising and left their honour behind, and at the caster's word five of the dead get up to fight for him.

necronomicon.name: The Necronomicon
necronomicon.unidentified_name: a book bound in human flesh
necronomicon.lore: The mad poet Abdul Alhazred wrote this book at Damascus under the title Al Azif, and was afterward devoured alive in the marketplace by a thing that none could see. So H. P. Lovecraft told in his stories of the 1920s, though he swore that he had made it all up, and librarians have been asked for the Necronomicon ever since. Yet here it lies, bound in something that is not calfskin, and let no one read it aloud, for the dead know when it is read and will answer.

sefer_yetzirah.name: Sefer Yetzirah (The Book of Formation)
sefer_yetzirah.lore: To Abraham tradition ascribes the Sefer Yetzirah, the Book of Formation, which is but a few pages long and among the oldest books of the Jewish mystics. It teaches that God formed the world by thirty-two paths of wisdom, which are the ten numbers and the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet. In Prague they tell how the great Rabbi Loew by those letters raised a man of clay to guard the ghetto, and whoever learns the working of this book will raise a guardian likewise.

picatrix.name: Picatrix
picatrix.lore: A sage of Muslim Spain gathered this book together in Arabic and called it Ghayat al-Hakim, the Aim of the Sage, and in 1256 King Alfonso the Wise of Castile had it turned into Spanish and then into Latin, under the name of Picatrix. For four centuries scholars read in secret how the powers of the planets may be drawn down into graven images. This working calls upon Mars, and every enemy in sight burns.

lemegeton.name: Lemegeton (The Lesser Key of Solomon)
lemegeton.unidentified_name: a black tome sealed with sigils
lemegeton.lore: King Solomon, the tale goes, shut seventy-two spirits in a vessel of brass, and the Ars Goetia, first of the five books that are bound together as the Lemegeton or Lesser Key of Solomon, gives for each a seal, a rank and a use. Bael makes men invisible and Vassago finds what is lost, and every one of them is a liar. Samuel Mathers translated it and Aleister Crowley printed it in 1904, but in this deep place it is the dead who answer its call, and five of them will come.

book_of_thoth.name: Book of Thoth
book_of_thoth.unidentified_name: a heavy book bound in papyrus and gold
book_of_thoth.lore: Thoth hid this book beneath the Nile in a box of iron in a box of bronze in a box of ebony in a box of ivory in a box of silver in a box of gold, and he set a serpent that cannot die to guard it. Whoever reads it once shall know all that the world holds that day, but whoever reads it wrongly shall lose the pieces of knowledge that he had before.

spellbook_acid_splash.name: Spellbook of Acid Splash
spellbook_acid_splash.lore: John Ray the naturalist wrote in 1671 of a sour, sharp spirit distilled from a great heap of red ants, and it is named formic acid from formica, the ant, whose bite owes its smart to that venom. A splash of the same is the first lesson in acids, and it stings, and the sting is slow to leave.

spellbook_corrosion.name: Spellbook of Corrosion
spellbook_corrosion.lore: A cliff of rock closed the road to Hannibal as he brought his army down from the Alps in 218 BC, and Livy tells how the soldiers felled trees and kindled a great fire against the stone, and poured sour wine upon it while it was hot until it crumbled and they could hew a road for the elephants. As that wine ate the mountain, this spell eats through whatever stands in the way.

spellbook_breath_of_boreas.name: Spellbook of Breath of Boreas
spellbook_breath_of_boreas.lore: The people of Athens called Boreas their son-in-law, since the North Wind had carried off Oreithyia their princess, and when the Persian fleet lay off Magnesia in 480 BC they prayed to their kinsman for aid. He came in a gale from the north and wrecked four hundred ships in three days. These pages loose that wind within a single room, and every enemy in sight must feel its breath.

spellbook_call_lightning.name: Spellbook of Call Lightning
spellbook_call_lightning.lore: Benjamin Franklin sent up a kite of silk into a thunderstorm in 1752 with a key upon the wet string, and sparks sprang from the key to his knuckle, whereby men knew that lightning and electricity were one. But Georg Richmann attempted the same a year later at St Petersburg, and the fire came down his rod and slew him. He who reads this tome calls it down by his own will, along a line toward his enemy.

spellbook_life_tap.name: Spellbook of Life Tap
spellbook_life_tap.lore: One evening near Coquimbo in Chile, as Charles Darwin lay encamped, his servant marked a restless horse and, laying a hand upon its back, caught a vampire bat that had made a small cut and was lapping there, though the horse had scarcely felt it. So quietly does the first lesson in draining take a little life from a foe within reach.

spellbook_vampiric_touch.name: Spellbook of Vampiric Touch
spellbook_vampiric_touch.lore: Johann Fluckinger, a surgeon of the Austrian army, was sent in 1732 to the Serbian village of Medvedja, where it was said that the soldier Arnold Paole, five years dead, had risen to drink the blood of his neighbours. The graves were opened and the bodies found fresh, and from his report all Europe learned the word vampire. The student of this book takes that same thirst into his own hand.

spellbook_enervation.name: Spellbook of Enervation
spellbook_enervation.lore: None could slay the demon Raktabija, for from every drop of his blood that touched the ground another Raktabija arose, until the field was full of him. Then the goddess Kali spread her tongue over all the battle and drank each drop before it fell, and so at last he died. Thus the last spell of draining leaves nothing to rise again.

spellbook_sacred_flame.name: Spellbook of Sacred Flame
spellbook_sacred_flame.lore: The High King of Ireland had forbidden, so they tell, that any fire be lit on Easter Eve before his own was kindled at Tara. But Saint Patrick lit the Paschal fire on the Hill of Slane in sight of all, and the druids warned the king that unless it were quenched that night it would never be quenched in Ireland. The first lesson of holy magic is to kindle a flame as small as his.

spellbook_holy_bolt.name: Spellbook of Holy Bolt
spellbook_holy_bolt.lore: For forty days Goliath of Gath, six cubits and a span in height and clad in scales of bronze, defied the host of Israel, until David the shepherd refused the king's armour, chose five smooth stones from the brook and slung one into the giant's forehead, so that he fell upon his face. This spell is that stone, and no armour turns it.

spellbook_flame_strike.name: Spellbook of Flame Strike
spellbook_flame_strike.lore: Elijah stood alone on Mount Carmel while the prophets of Baal cried to their god from morning until noon and no fire came. Then he built his altar, had it drenched three times with water and prayed once, and fire fell from heaven, consuming offering, wood, stones and dust and licking up the water in the trench. With these words one calls down that fire upon a single enemy.

spellbook_judgment.name: Spellbook of Judgment
spellbook_judgment.lore: The Book of Revelation tells of war in heaven, how Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, that old serpent who is called the Devil and Satan, and how the dragon was overcome and cast down to the earth with all his angels. The sentence of Michael is the last of the holy spells, and it spares nothing that stands against it.

spellbook_galdr_of_loosing.name: Spellbook of Galdr of Loosing
spellbook_galdr_of_loosing.lore: Odin had a charm for a man in chains, and it was his boast that when he sang it the fetters sprang from the feet and the cuffs from the hands, so that there was no captive in the North but longed to know it. Sung in the dungeon it breaks root, web and grip, and for a few breaths nothing can take hold again.

spellbook_cockcrow.name: Spellbook of Cockcrow
spellbook_cockcrow.lore: It was believed of old that the dead walk only until the cock crow, and that at his call every wandering spirit must seek its grave. Prudentius made a hymn of it for the dawn in the fourth century, and the ghost in Hamlet fades at the sound. This spell is that first crow, called before its hour.

spellbook_sanctuary.name: Spellbook of Sanctuary
spellbook_sanctuary.lore: A hunted man in medieval England had but to reach a church and lay hold upon the ring of its door, which at Durham was a lion's head of bronze on the north side, and his pursuers must wait without and could not drag him away. The reader of these words raises that old law about himself for a little while, and like the law it shelters no one who fights.

spellbook_elf_shot.name: Spellbook of Elf-Shot
spellbook_elf_shot.lore: When man or beast was taken with sudden pains, the Anglo-Saxons knew that the elves had loosed their tiny arrows, which no eye sees in flight, and wrote charms against elf-shot in their leechbooks and treasured as elven darts the flints turned up in their fields. The spell borrows one such dart, and its target stiffens where it stands.

spellbook_stayed_spear.name: Spellbook of Galdr of the Stayed Spear
spellbook_stayed_spear.lore: On the windy tree Odin won the charms that are numbered in the Havamal, and the fifth is this, that if he sees a spear in flight toward him, however strongly thrown, he can stay it in the air. Such galdr is sung and never written, and the singer must watch the shaft, for what he sees coming falls short, but what he does not see will find him still.

spellbook_tacitas_seal.name: Spellbook of Tacita's Seal
spellbook_tacitas_seal.lore: While the Romans fed their dead, an old woman would sit among the girls making her offering to Tacita, the goddess who cannot speak. She sewed up a fish's mouth, sealed it with pitch and roasted it, saying that she had bound all hostile tongues. When her seal is set upon one creature, its mouth works but nothing comes out.

spellbook_dionysus_vine.name: Spellbook of Dionysus's Vine
spellbook_dionysus_vine.lore: Certain pirates of the Tyrrhenian sea seized a youth upon the shore for a rich king's son, but when they would bind him the ropes fell away, wine ran over the deck, vine climbed the sail and ivy wound the mast until the ship could not move, for he was Dionysus. A little of that god's green anger may be called out of the stones, to hold fast as it held the ship.

spellbook_shrink_the_earth.name: Spellbook of Shrink the Earth
spellbook_shrink_the_earth.lore: An old seller of medicines who lived inside a gourd took Fei Changfang for his pupil and taught him the arts of the immortals, until he could fold the veins of the earth, the storytellers say, and make a town a thousand li away but a step distant. The spell folds less ground, and brings within one stride what the caster can see close by.

spellbook_bough_of_somnus.name: Spellbook of Bough of Somnus
spellbook_bough_of_somnus.lore: On the last night of the voyage to Italy the god of Sleep came to Palinurus, the helmsman of Aeneas, in the likeness of a friend, and when the man would not leave the tiller the god shook over his brows a bough wet with the dew of Lethe, until his eyes closed. This spell shakes the same bough above a knot of foes.

spellbook_dulled_blades.name: Spellbook of Galdr of Dulled Blades
spellbook_dulled_blades.lore: The third of Odin's charms was a war-song, and when he sang it against his foes their swords grew blunt and their staves soft, so that nothing they swung would bite him. The fighters of the North carved such songs on their shields, but this one is sung over a whole room at once.

spellbook_confusion_of_tongues.name: Spellbook of Confusion of Tongues
spellbook_confusion_of_tongues.lore: The whole earth had once a single tongue, as Genesis tells, and the builders of Babel thought to raise a tower to heaven, but God came down and confounded their speech, so that no man understood his neighbour and the work was left and the builders were scattered. These words work the same ruin on a band of foes, for each hears his fellows babble and must fight alone.

spellbook_darkness_of_egypt.name: Spellbook of Darkness of Egypt
spellbook_darkness_of_egypt.lore: Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, as Exodus tells, and there fell on Egypt a darkness so thick that it might be felt. For three days none saw another or rose from his place, though in the houses of Israel there was light. So this spell brings the darkness upon every foe in sight, and the caster's own eyes are left clear.

spellbook_pans_panic.name: Spellbook of Pan's Panic
spellbook_pans_panic.lore: As Pheidippides ran upon his errand before Marathon, the god Pan met him on the mountain road and asked why Athens did him no honour, who had ever been its helper. When the Persians had broken and fled, the Athenians made him a shrine beneath the Acropolis, and the sudden, senseless terror that takes a multitude bears his name still.

spellbook_settled_strife.name: Spellbook of Galdr of Settled Strife
spellbook_settled_strife.lore: When hatred rose among the sons of a war-leader and a hall was near to blows, Odin had a song that would make their hands fall from their sword hilts, and the skalds held the peace of a king more precious than his army. It has power upon all who are able to hate, and therefore none upon the beasts or upon the dead.

spellbook_mist_of_manannan.name: Spellbook of Mist of Manannan
spellbook_mist_of_manannan.lore: Whenever raiders drew near the Isle of Man, so the Manx say, Manannan mac Lir the lord of the sea spread his cloak of mist over all the island and their ships sailed by. The old gods of the Irish named that veil the feth fiada, and by it were hidden from mortal sight. Called down in the dungeon, it lets a creature see only what is right beside it.

spellbook_hush_of_the_feralia.name: Spellbook of Hush of the Feralia
spellbook_hush_of_the_feralia.lore: The folk of Rome bore food to the tombs of their fathers on the Feralia and spoke there softly, while old women made offering to the silent goddess, for on that one day the city hushed for its dead. Here the same hush is laid upon a whole room, so that each mouth in it works without a sound.
